bull.b: Royal Caribbean has rebuilt substantial profitability and scale, with strong margins and net income far above post-downturn levels. This creates internal funding capacity for fleet, destination, technology, and guest-experience investments while strengthening resilience across the travel cycle.

Record pricing, healthy booking volumes, and rising advance purchases indicate durable demand and stronger guest monetization. Higher ticket yields and ancillary spending can support revenue growth without relying solely on capacity expansion, improving the economics of each sailing.

The Sandals partnership broadens Royal Caribbean beyond ocean cruising into established Caribbean resort brands serving adults and families. The combined platform may enable cross-selling, deepen loyalty engagement, and diversify vacation revenue while extending the company’s destination presence.

bear.b: Although leverage has improved materially from its 2022 peak, the debt burden remains significant relative to equity. That structure leaves Royal Caribbean more exposed to demand slowdowns, refinancing conditions, and interest expense, limiting flexibility if the travel cycle weakens.

Strong operating cash flow has not translated into positive free cash flow after investment and working-capital effects. Persistent cash conversion pressure could constrain debt reduction, fleet and destination investment, and shareholder returns, particularly while leverage remains elevated.

The business remains sensitive to travel demand, itinerary mix, and operating costs. Europe booking disruption and higher per-capacity costs can moderate yields and margins, showing that earnings growth may remain volatile when geopolitical events or deployment changes affect customer decisions.
